{"report": "# Matter Smart-Home Standard: Executive Brief

## What it is
Matter is a technical standard for smart-home and IoT devices. It aims to improve interoperability between manufacturers, strengthen security, and always allow local control. It began in December 2019 as "Project CHIP", founded by Amazon, Apple, Google, Samsung SmartThings and the Zigbee Alliance, now the Connectivity Standards Alliance (CSA). IKEA, Huawei, Schneider and others have since joined. Version 1.0 was published on 4 October 2022.

## How it works
- **IP-based application layer.** Matter runs over Wi-Fi, Ethernet and Thread, the three officially supported networks.
- **Local control.** Controllers manage devices on the local network. This removes the need for a separate proprietary hub per ecosystem, and core functions work without an internet connection.
- **Expanding scope.** Version 1.0 covered lighting, plugs, switches, door locks, thermostats/HVAC, blinds, security sensors and TVs/streamers. Version 1.2 (October 2023) added refrigerators, dishwashers, washers, robot vacuums, smoke/CO alarms, air-quality sensors, air purifiers, fans and portable air conditioners. The CSA plans updates twice a year.

## Why it matters for device makers
1. **Build once, reach multiple ecosystems.** One certified product can work with the major ecosystems (Apple, Google, Amazon, Samsung). This reduces ecosystem-specific integration work and fragmentation.
2. **Lower barrier to a broad market.** Consumers can recognise the Matter logo, which the CSA hopes will signal that a product will "just work".
3. **Category expansion.** Appliance makers now have defined device types to build to.
4. **Differentiation shifts upward.** Basic connectivity becomes a commodity. Competition moves to app experience, services and reliability. *(This is our inference, not a claim from the source.)*

{"report": "# A High-Level Overview of "Everything"

## Scope and Limits
"Everything" can't be covered in a short report. This report reads it in two ways: **everything that exists** (the universe) and **everything humans know** (how knowledge is organized). It is a broad orientation, not an exhaustive account. It rests on two Wikipedia pages, and only part of each page's text was retrieved because the text was truncated. The cosmic composition figures come from the ΛCDM model. That model is widely accepted, but it is still a model.

## Part 1: The Universe
The universe is all matter, energy, space and time, along with the structures they form, from subatomic particles to galactic filaments.

**Age and size**
- Cosmology indicates the universe has been expanding for about **13.8 billion years**, starting from a dense fireball in the Big Bang.
- The observable universe is roughly **93 billion light-years** across. The total size is unknown.

**Structure**
- The Sun is one of a few hundred billion stars in the Milky Way. The Milky Way is one of a few hundred billion galaxies in the observable universe.
- At the largest scales, galaxies form clusters and superclusters. These are arranged in filaments around voids, giving a foam-like structure.

**Composition (ΛCDM model)**

| Component | Share of universe |
|---|---|
| Dark energy | ~69.2% |
| Dark matter | ~25.8% |
| Ordinary (baryonic) matter | ~4.84% |

Stars, planets and visible gas make up only about 6% of the ordinary matter.

**Changing models**
Understanding has moved from Earth-centered (geocentric) models to the Sun-centered (heliocentric) model during the Scientific Revolution. General relativity and other early 20th-century discoveries then led to the modern expanding-universe picture.

**Open questions**
The ultimate fate of the universe is still debated. So is what, if anything, preceded the Big Bang.

{"report": "# A Brief History of the Internet: ARPANET, the Web, and the 21st Century

## 1. Origins and ARPANET (1960s–1990)
The internet grew from efforts to build and interconnect computer networks. In the late 1950s, J. C. R. Licklider of ARPA described a universal network. In the early 1960s, Paul Baran (RAND) proposed a distributed network built on message blocks. In 1965, Donald Davies (UK National Physical Laboratory) independently conceived packet switching.

Bob Taylor began ARPANET in 1966, with Larry Roberts as program manager. In 1969, Bolt Beranek & Newman won the contract to build the Interface Message Processors, with Bob Kahn leading the design. UCLA graduate students led by Steve Crocker, including Jon Postel, specified the host protocol. The network was declared operational in 1971 and supported remote login, file transfer and early email.

Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published their internetworking research in 1974. It became TCP/IP and drew on France's CYCLADES project and Bob Metcalfe's Ethernet. ARPANET adopted TCP/IP on 1 January 1983. The NSF then funded CSNET (1981) and NSFNET (1986), and the Domain Name System appeared. Commercial ISPs emerged in 1989. ARPANET was decommissioned in 1990, and the NSFNET backbone followed in 1995, which removed the last restrictions on commercial use.

## 2. The World Wide Web (1989–early 2000s)
The Web is a service that runs on the internet, not the internet itself. Tim Berners-Lee proposed a "universal linked information system" at CERN in 1989. He built the first server, the first browser and HTML. The markup language was published in 1991, and the browser code was released publicly in 1993.
